content.title: CDC Warns Drug-Resistant Shigella Infections Are Rising in the U.S.
content.text: Shigella symptoms include diarrhea, fever and stomach pain, and the CDC is calling it “a public health threat" Stock photo of person with abdominal pain. Credit : Getty NEED TO KNOW The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention stated that drug-resistant shigella infections have increased 8.5% in the United States from 2011 to 2023Shigellosis is spread between people through fecal-oral transmission, sexual contact or contaminated food and waterSymptoms include diarrhea, fever and stomach pain A drug-resistant strain of shigella infections is increasing in the United States. An Thursday, April 9, report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) stated that drug-resistant shigella infections, which cause diarrhea, have increased 8.5% in the United States from 2011 to 2023. According to the Mayo Clinic, the infection is spread between people through fecal-oral transmission, sexual contact or contaminated food and water. Sign for Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Getty Historically, shigella was susceptible to antibiotics that killed the infection. But officials stated that this drug-resistant strain is resistant to the antibiotics ampicillin, azithromycin, ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. There is no Food and Drug Administration–approved oral treatment for these infections, according to the CDC. Officials analyzed over 16,700 shigella samples from January 2011 to October 2023 and found that the number of drug-resistant infections increased from 0% in 2011-2015 to 8.5% in 2023. The first drug-resistant strain was identified in 2016. Most patients were adult men and the median age was 41. Of those who provided travel history, 82.4% reported no recent international travel. Stock image of shigella bacteria. KATERYNA KON/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY / Getty Images Related Stories Symptoms of a shigella infection include diarrhea that may be bloody or last more than three days, fever and stomach pain, per the Mayo Clinic. Once infected, symptoms typically start within one or two days and usually last between five to seven days, although some cases last longer. Anyone with a weakened immune system should contact their doctor if they are experiencing symptoms. Additionally, those with high fevers, bloody diarrhea, frequent vomiting or dehydration symptoms should also seek medical assistance, the Mayo Clinic advises. Children, travelers, people who have anal sex and people experiencing homelessness are more likely to be infected. For prevention, the CDC recommends washing hands often, avoiding swallowing water when swimming, following safe food and water habits when traveling and not having sex for at least two weeks if infected.
